title: US Oil Refiners Post Record Profits as Iran War Drives Margins to All-Time Highs
excerpt: Marathon Petroleum, Valero, and Phillips 66 earned a combined $12.6 billion in Q2 and returned $6.3 billion to shareholders, the most in over two years.
body:
• The three largest US independent refiners — Marathon, Phillips 66, and Valero — earned combined profits of $12.6 billion in Q2 2026, the most since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022
  • The 3-2-1 crack spread hit a record $69.66 per barrel, while the diesel crack spread reached $93.84 on August 10
  • Refiners returned $6.3 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends in Q2, up from $2.6 billion a year ago
  • Marathon shares are up approximately 110% year-to-date; Valero has gained over 98% and Phillips 66 about 75%

War-Driven Margins Shatter Records

America's largest oil refiners have posted their biggest profits in years as the Iran war continues to reshape global energy markets, sending the cost of turning crude oil into fuel to unprecedented levels.

Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66, and Valero Energy earned a combined $12.6 billion in the second quarter, according to Reuters — the largest haul since Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted energy markets in 2022. The three companies returned $6.3 billion to shareholders through stock repurchases and dividends, more than double the $2.6 billion distributed during the same period last year.

"To say that they made a lot of cash is an understatement," said Gabelli Funds portfolio manager Simon Wong.

Crack Spreads Hit Records

Refining margins, measured by so-called crack spreads — the difference between crude oil costs and the price of refined fuels — have surged to record territory. The benchmark 3-2-1 crack spread, which approximates the margin from turning three barrels of crude into two barrels of gasoline and one of diesel, rose to $69.66 per barrel, a record high. The average 3-2-1 spread from 2018 to 2025 was $23.19, according to OPIS.

Diesel margins have been particularly extreme. The ultra-low sulfur diesel futures crack spread jumped to a record $93.84 per barrel on August 10, driven by years of constrained global refining capacity, a Russian ban on most diesel exports following months of Ukrainian drone attacks on the country's refineries, and renewed tension around the Strait of Hormuz.

Massive Shareholder Returns

The windfall profits have translated directly into aggressive shareholder return programs. Phillips 66's board approved a $10 billion increase to its share repurchase program in July. Valero authorized a new $5 billion buyback on top of the remaining capacity under a prior $2.5 billion program. Smaller rival HF Sinclair raised its quarterly dividend by 5%.

"We think the buyback programs will continue to be pretty robust for Valero and Marathon."

— Jason Gabelman, TD Cowen analyst

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman estimated that Marathon and Valero will each repurchase roughly 20% of their market value between the third quarter and the end of next year. Marathon is currently valued at approximately $91.3 billion and Valero at around $90.1 billion. Phillips 66, which is prioritizing growth investments and debt reduction, is expected to buy back about 10% of its $81.2 billion market cap.

Stock Prices Reflect the Boom

Year-to-date, Marathon shares have surged roughly 110% to around $342. Valero has gained more than 98%, while Phillips 66 is up approximately 75%. All three have dramatically outperformed the S&P 500 energy sector, which has risen about 36% over the same period.

US gasoline prices have climbed above $4 a gallon at the pump, and refineries are running at 96% of capacity — well above the typical 92% to 94% range. Refiners are also exporting 10% to 20% of their output, roughly double normal levels, as international buyers scramble for supply.

Cautious Optimism Ahead

Refining executives signaled cautious optimism for the second half, which typically brings seasonal weakness as the market transitions between summer driving season and winter heating demand. Product margins remain robust but have eased from peak second-quarter levels, according to Marathon chief commercial officer Rick Hessling.

Valero's jet fuel margins have weakened in the early third quarter, but an arbitrage window for jet fuel exports to Europe has reopened, and COO Gary Simmons expects margins to strengthen as refiners switch to winter diesel specifications. Analysts expect the industry's run of elevated profitability to continue into at least the third quarter.
